idiom_name: three sequential beats in the test body (arrange / act / assert), marked by comments, blocks or a runner
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: establish the fixture first (state, collaborators, inputs), then perform exactly one call or interaction, then check the observable outcome - the returned value, the post-state, the raised error or the recorded interaction. Mark the three beats with comments or the framework's block vocabulary so that a second act, or an assertion inside the arrange beat, is visible in review; keep fixture work every test needs in the runner's before-each hook and put test-specific state back into the test body. Prefer one assertion about the behaviour - equality style, naming expected and actual - over a colour of boolean flags, and let teardown happen through the after-each hook or RAII rather than inside the assert path. In exception tests, wrap the act in a raises block to combine act-and-assert naturally.
code_sketch:
# Arrange
account = Account(balance=100)

# Act
ok = account.withdraw(30)

# Assert
assert ok
assert account.balance == 70
pitfalls: Ritual beats: the marker comments are present but the code still interleaves arrangement, several acts and assertions.
Fixture growth: everything accumulates in the before-each hook until the test body no longer says what makes this test distinct.
Assertions placed in the arrange beat turn a fixture defect into a failure that reads like a behaviour defect.
A boolean-only assert hides the actual value and makes the failure message useless.
Multiple acts in one test, where a failure cannot be localised to a single behaviour without investigation.
